slides.notes: Built from Ian's story map method, version 5 (knowledge layer, plus the activities, tasks and details protocols), and doc 11. Worked example: the DMV License Ready Check.

slides.html:
Why we map

A story map shows how people accomplish their goals, step by step, using what we build.

Understand the journey

In clear, sequential terms, from the first need to done.

Build shared understanding

Between everyone working on it, people and AI alike.

Organize the work

From high-level goals down to what we can actually build.

Decide what comes first

Slice the map across to plan releases.

Now maps

Capture how people do it today. Use them in discovery to see where the pain is.

Later maps

Picture how people will do it with what we build. Use them to slice a Solution into Deliverables.

Same structure, same process. Only the time frame changes.
slides.notes: From the v5 method. Mapping happens when a Solution moves to Next on the roadmap, with the people who did the discovery.

slides.html:
Three levels, from abstract to buildable

Activities

Solution-agnostic human goals

What people are trying to accomplish. No technology.

"Complete registration"

Tasks

Solution-implied capabilities

The single actions that get it done. Still needs interpreting to build.

"Submit registration form"

Details

Concrete buildable units

Specific enough to build. The smallest piece you can describe from the user's side.

"Upload supporting documents"

You cannot build from an Activity. It's too abstract. Details are what get built and delivered in releases.
slides.notes: The examples on the right are the government portal example from the v5 method. Activities and tasks together form the backbone of the map.

slides.html:
Activities: the big stages

Something a person would say they accomplished: "I finished our travel plans."

  • A stage people recognize as a group of related actions, not one step
  • People might pause or switch context before finishing it
  • A broad verb phrase: Plan, Manage, Prepare
  • Solution-agnostic: no buttons, forms, screens or uploads
  • 3 to 8 per map, all the same size of goal, covering the whole journey

Too specific: these are tasks

Activities

Enter Destination

Plan Trip

Request Ride

Get Transportation

Track Driver

Track Journey

Create Board

Capture Work

Unsure if it's an Activity or a Task? Lean toward the Activity, the higher level.
slides.notes: From the activities protocol. If it mentions a specific digital action or interface element, it is too specific to be an Activity.

slides.html:
Tasks: the single actions

Something a person would say they did: "I found our flight price."

Too abstract (Activity)

Just right (Task)

Too specific (Detail)

Get Transportation

Request Ride

Enter destination address

Plan Vacation

Search Flights

Select departure airport

Get Cleaned Up

Take Shower

Adjust water temperature

Coordinate Work

Create Board

Click "New Board" button

The rules

Clear start and end; nobody stops halfway. An action verb phrase. 3 to 7 per Activity, in the order people do them.

The test

If the step can be split into smaller describable actions, those are details.
slides.notes: From the tasks protocol. Tasks are solution-implied but not solution-specific: no UI language, no implementation specifics.

slides.html:
Details: what people accomplish, not what they click

This is where most maps go wrong, including most maps AI writes.

Avoid interaction verbs

Click, tap, press, swipe. See, view, display. Enter, type, input. Select, choose. Drag, drop, scroll. Open, close, toggle.

Use outcome verbs

Know, understand, verify, confirm. Specify, set, define. Compare, filter, find. Track, monitor. Control, manage, adjust.

Interaction-focused

Outcome-focused

Click 'Request Ride' button

Confirm ride request

See estimated arrival time

Know estimated arrival time before confirming

Enter departure city

Specify departure point for flight search

View driver photo

Verify driver identity and reputation

Drag card to 'Done' column

Mark work as complete
slides.notes: From the v5 knowledge layer. Some "see" is fine when the information itself is the value: "See driver location on map" is valid; "See modal dialog" is not.

slides.html:
The "So that what?" test

Ask: the person does this... so that what?

"So they can click another button"

Or "so they can see something." It's interaction-focused. Rewrite it.

A meaningful outcome or capability

It's outcome-focused. Keep it.

It also sizes a detail

A detail is the right size when it reads as "As a [user], I want [action], so that [benefit]," and splitting it further gives pieces with the same "so that."

"Log in with Google" is one detail, not "enter email," "click button" and "redirect." All three serve the same benefit: so that I don't have to create and remember another login.
slides.notes: This is the test the system uses for stories too: if two pieces share the same "so that," they were one story.

slides.html:
Five ways a detail goes wrong

Generate freely, then review for these, then fix only what's broken.

UI mechanics

"Tap map to set location"

"Specify pickup location"

Performance goals

"Load board quickly"

"Progressive rendering for large boards" (target under 2 seconds as a note)

Emotional outcomes

"Feel satisfied moving a card"

"Visual feedback when a card moves to Done"

Vague aspirations

"Easy to understand"

"Example cards showing usage"

Design constraints

"Create board without setup steps"

"Board created with sensible defaults"

The fix is always the same question: what specifically makes this true? Build that.
slides.notes: From the details protocol, v2: generate, review, refine. Keep details that are already good; make surgical fixes, not wholesale rewrites. A performance target or a feeling is a valid design goal; record it as a note, not as a detail.

slides.html:
The map is a grid

Left to right is the order people act. Top to bottom is the order we deliver.

Get Cleaned Up

 

 

Get Dressed

 

Leave Home

Take a Shower

Brush Teeth

Shave

Choose Clothes

Put On Clothes

Lock Up

RELEASE 1: Get out the door on time

Adjust water to a comfortable temperature

Clean teeth

 

Pick an outfit for the weather

Lay out clothes the night before

Know the door is locked

LATER

Handle sudden temperature changes

 

Shave without nicks

 

 

 

Activities

Appear once, above their first task. Never repeated.

Tasks

One per column, in the order people do them.

Details and releases

Details stack under their task. Release lines cut across the whole map.
slides.notes: Layout rules from the v5 visual guidelines: identical card sizes, columns that line up, empty spaces kept so the grid never collapses. The morning routine is the method's own teaching example; the details here are simplified for the slide.

slides.html:
Releases start with a target outcome

What will people be able to do once this ships?

Write the outcome first

A user-focused statement of a new behavior or ability. "Users can request a basic ride with confidence."

Then pick the details

Only the details that make that outcome possible. Everything else moves below the line.

Cut across the whole map

A release can span many activities and tasks, but it must work end to end for someone.

Leave the activities in place

Even when nothing under an activity makes this release. The gap shows what this release won't do.
slides.notes: Releases reference details, not tasks, because details are what get built. From the v5 knowledge layer and doc 11.

slides.html:
A release is a vertical slice

In our system, each release slice scheduled into a quarter is a Deliverable.

Horizontal: a phase

Database this quarter, screens next quarter. Nobody can use it, so nobody can tell us if it's right.

Vertical: a slice

A thin path through every layer that works end to end for someone. We can demo it to a real user and learn.

The test

Can you demo it to a real user and get useful feedback? If not, it's a horizontal piece.

Learning slices

Some slices test the riskiest assumption with real users, often by hand or behind a flag, before we build the rest.
slides.notes: From doc 11. A Deliverable someone can't use is a phase, not a slice. A vertical-versus-horizontal slices picture would do the job of the two top cards.

slides.html:
From a detail to a story

Each detail in the current slice becomes one or more user stories.

Send a document for review

Submit a birth certificate photo

STORY

As a first-time applicant, I need to submit a photo of my birth certificate before my visit, so that I can know it will be accepted without making a trip.

Given I started a License Ready Check, when I upload a JPG, PNG or PDF under 10 MB, then I see "Received. Staff will review it within 2 business days."

Split by user path, never by layer

The first version covered every document type and was estimated at 13. The team split it by document type.

Group into epics if it helps

By map column, by document type, or the whole slice. The one rule: an epic stays inside one Solution.
slides.notes: Story 1 from the user story template. From here the sprint deck takes over: definition of ready, refinement, spikes.

slides.html:
Coherence, not perfection

Gray areas are normal. Is "Categorize Cards" a task, or a detail of "Organize Work"?

Every Activity

should feel like the same kind of big stage.

Every Task

should feel like the same kind of single action.

Every Detail

should feel like the same kind of buildable unit.

The 90% rule

If you are less than 90% sure which level something belongs at, ask rather than guess. That goes for people and for AI building a map with us.
slides.notes: Different maps can make different classification choices. What matters is consistency inside one map.

slides.html:
Who maps, and when

When

When a Solution moves to Next on the roadmap. Slice releases by target outcome, then schedule each slice into a quarter as a Deliverable.

With whom

The people who did the discovery. Use the words users use.

Roles

  • Product owner facilitates mapping and slicing
  • Product manager sets each slice's target outcome
  • UX designer and researcher brings users' steps and words
  • Development team splits and estimates
  • Technical architect names dependencies
  • Content strategist joins when words or rules change
slides.notes: From doc 11. AI can draft a map from discovery notes using the v5 protocols; the team reviews it with the anti-pattern list.

slides.html:
Rules of thumb

Map in the order people act.

Left to right is their journey, not our org chart.

Activities have no technology in them.

If it names a button or a form, it's a task or a detail.

Details are outcomes, not clicks.

Ask "so that what?"

Every release starts with a target outcome.

Then pick only the details that make it true.

Keep skipped activities on the map.

The gap shows what this release won't do.

If you can't demo it, it isn't a slice.

A Deliverable someone can't use is a phase.
slides.notes: Close with a practice round: map one service the team knows well, today's way (a Now map), in 30 minutes. [Pick the service].
